In total, 331 simultaneous meteors were detected across the two observation campaigns - 145 in ICCD09 and 228 in KISO18.
The relationship between radar cross section and optical V-band magnitude was well approximated by a linear function.
A transformation function from radar cross section to V-band magnitude was derived for sporadic meteors.
The mass range of meteors detected by the MU radar was constrained to about 10^-5 to 10^0 grams.
The luminosity function of sporadic meteors detected by the MU radar was well approximated by a single power-law function with a population index of r = 3.52 ± 0.12.
In ICCD09, the detected meteors ranged from 1.4 to 10.0 magnitude, with 25-75 percentile magnitudes of 5.0 to 7.2.
In KISO18, the detected meteors ranged from 2.8 to 11.1 magnitude, with 25-75 percentile magnitudes of 7.4 to 8.6.
The altitudes of the KISO18 meteors were generally lower than those of the ICCD09 meteors, due to the displaced pointing of the Tomo-e Gozen telescope below 30 degrees elevation.
The archival MU radar meteor observations from 2009-2015 were analyzed to derive the luminosity function of faint sporadic meteors, covering the magnitude range of -1.5 to 9.5.
Faint meteors corresponding to radar head echo observations, as faint as 10 magnitude optically, had not been detected until recently due to insufficient sensitivity of optical observations.
The simultaneous radar and optical observations helped constrain the luminous efficiency and ionization coefficient of meteors.
The MU radar is capable of detecting interplanetary dust of 10^-5 to 10^0 grams in mass as meteors.
The observations were carried out using the MU radar and optical cameras - an image-intensified CCD camera in ICCD09 and the Tomo-e Gozen mosaic CMOS camera in KISO18.
The Tomo-e Gozen camera has a large field-of-view of about 20 square degrees and can monitor the sky at 2 Hz.
The observations were biased towards meteor showers like Geminids, Orionids, and η Aquariids, which were removed from the analysis of sporadic meteors.
